source: Semantic Scholar Graph API, /paper/DOI:…/citations?fields=contexts,intents,isInfluential,citingPaper.title,citingPaper.year,citingPaper.venue, pulled 2026-10-02 in the browser; every citation record that carries at least one citing sentence was read (the longest sentence, and the second where present); records without a sentence are not classified. Semantic Scholar's sentence extraction covers open-access full texts, so the 1990s subscription-journal citers are under-represented. Lindzen et al. 2001 was not done: its index record is split between the paper and the Hartmann & Michelsen 2002 comment and holds few sentences before 2010.

classes.S: adopts the claim as support or as a live estimate (the authors' own group and their replies included)
classes.O: treats the question as open: 'debate', 'controversy', 'uncertain', 'has been suggested', the claim used as one scenario or perspective
classes.R: argues or tests against the claim, or sets it aside ('speculations… but most studies today favor'); a known direct test of the record is R even where the citing sentence is a method citation
classes.H: narrates the dispute as history: 'once suggested', 'the debate initiated by', 'at the time', 'early work showed'
classes.M: cites the paper for something other than the claim: a mechanism, a radiative fact, a method, a dataset
classes.X: noise: off-topic use, index error (the sentence cites a different paper), non-article

method: Class by the citing sentence first; where the sentence is a bare method or data citation but the citing paper is a known direct test of the claim (Wentz & Schabel 1998; Mears et al. 2002, 2003; Fu et al. 2004; Fu & Johanson 2004) or by the contested paper's own authors, the paper's stance is used and the note says so. Duplicate index records (preprint + journal, two versions of one chapter) are kept as separate rows because they are separate records in the index; they are few and marked. 'id' is the first eight characters of the Semantic Scholar paperId.
